first.rationale: Both current declines (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%) point at the self-serve funnel, so memory_86 (shortened onboarding) is the most directly load-bearing inherited belief for the action I intend to take — and its recorded evidence is completion rate and time-to-value, which are proxies, not the qualified-revenue outcome I am actually optimizing. That combination (high consequence + support that does not reach the objective) makes it the top verification target. memory_73 (promotional pricing) is the second: the competitor's entry pricing makes it the loudest alternative, and its recorded support is acquisition and revenue lift with no evidence on retention, margin, or account quality, which is exactly the gap that matters for sustainable revenue. I did not spend budget on memory_57 or memory_44 because neither addresses the funnel stage that is degrading, and I did not verify memory_31 because it overlaps memory_86 and is the narrower claim; verifying the broader one is the better use of a scarce pull. Intended action is onboarding simplification at small guarded scale: it attacks the plausible common cause of both declines, whereas discounting responds to the competitor without fixing the funnel and risks buying price-sensitive, low-durability accounts. Explicit downstream risk: stripping onboarding steps can remove qualification and setup signals, so a completion-rate win can coexist with worse account quality — I will instrument first-value, week-4 retention and revenue quality, not just completion, and hold rollout until those read out. If the archive shows memory_86's lift was measured only on completion with no durability follow-up, or that memory_73's revenue lift held on retained cohorts, I will revise before committing.

mid.rationale: The archive resolved both open questions in the direction that settles this cycle. exp_86 did not stop at completion: +13% completion, -2.1 days time-to-value, and crucially +3% 30-day retention. That closes the proxy-vs-objective gap I flagged — the shortened flow did not buy completion by stripping qualification, since the accounts survived a month. exp_73 confirmed the failure mode I suspected: +31% signup and +18% qualified revenue are real but sit on top of -12% 30-day retention, and the source record explicitly warns against generalizing targeted discounting as sustainable growth. Under a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional pricing is now disqualified for this slot, not merely deprioritized; matching the competitor on price would buy a cohort that does not reach first renewal and would mask, not fix, the funnel decline. Committing the single slot to onboarding simplification: it is the one direction with verified durability evidence and it targets the plausible common cause of both the -4% completion and -6% activation declines. Raising from small guarded test to standard experiment because the retention evidence removed the specific risk that justified extra guarding — but not to broad rollout, since exp_86 ran in a different competitive environment, 30-day retention is still short of a renewal cycle, and today's activation drop may have a component onboarding does not touch. Guardrails held: instrument first-value, week-4 retention, and revenue quality per cohort alongside completion, and treat a completion lift without a retention lift as a stop signal rather than a win. Residual uncertainty: if activation stays depressed after onboarding recovers, the cause is downstream and activation_messaging (memory_91, still unverified) becomes the next slot's candidate.

final2.rationale: The competitive news raises urgency but changes no evidence. Nothing I learned this morning contradicts exp_73's finding that discount-acquired SMB cohorts churn out before first renewal (-12% 30-day retention against +18% qualified revenue), and nothing strengthens the case for spending the single slot on price. Holding the onboarding experiment at standard scale. One honest distinction I want on the record rather than buried: exp_73 tested acquisition discounting at price-sensitive SMB prospects, whereas leadership is now facing retention conversations with existing accounts. Defensive pricing to save accounts that already cleared qualification is not the same intervention and its durability is genuinely unknown to me — I should not overclaim that exp_73 rules it out. But unknown is not supported, and the one verified, durability-tested direction I have is the onboarding fix. Committing a scarce experiment slot to an untested variant of the one strategy whose closest recorded analogue failed on exactly the objective I am optimizing would be the wrong trade under deadline pressure. Two further reasons to hold: doubling churn conversations this week cannot be resolved by an experiment that reads out over weeks, so an experiment slot is the wrong instrument for an urgent retention problem regardless of direction; and matching a competitor into a second deeper cut invites a third, on a cost structure I have no evidence we win. The right response to today's churn calls is account-level commercial judgment by the team that owns those relationships — pricing exceptions, term changes, save offers — which does not consume the experiment slot and should be decided by leadership with margin data I do not hold. I am recommending that separation explicitly rather than letting the experiment slot substitute for it. Guardrails unchanged: track first-value, week-4 retention and per-cohort revenue quality, not completion alone; a completion lift without a retention lift is a stop signal. Residual uncertainty: if onboarding recovers and activation stays down, the cause is downstream and activation_messaging (memory_91, unverified) is next cycle's candidate; I would also spend a future archive pull on whether any retention-side pricing evidence exists before anyone treats defensive discounting as safe.
